title: Before AI - Nvidia's greatest technical achievements (and bombs)
text:
Xebec
Well-known member

An opinion piece, but I'd like to hear others thoughts. I've followed Nvidia for a long time (since 1996-7 when the game Unreal made me consider a new graphics card). From my perspective, here are some of Nvidia's greatest technical achievements:

- 1997: Nvidia Riva 128 chipset - although not Nvidia's first 3D chipset (that was the prior NV1), this put Nvidia on the roadmap with gamers offering 24-bit color while competition (3DFx voodoo) was often limited to 16-bit colors in 3D. This chip saved the company from bankruptcy.

- 2001: GeForce 2 Go - Nvidia's first dedicated mobile GPU.

- 2001-2004+: nForce chipsets - Nvidia entering the iGPU and chipset market at the same time created new (but somewhat short lived) opportunities

- 2007: CUDA - I remember receiving an early pitch of this (for work), and only a few high end 3D software products used CUDA. But when it was offered - it was a huge performance leap over CPUs at the time for very specialized tasks. CUDA is the foundation for all of Nvidia's success today, imo.

- 2014: Nvidia "Maxwell" second gen GPUs (900 series). Without a change in manufacturing process, Nvidia nearly doubled power efficiency for 3D and GPU CUDA tasks over the prior generation. AMD has never caught up in efficiency since this uplift.

Other mentions:

- Some will give credit to the Nvidia GeForce being the first GPU. IMO, there were many GPUs before this. (See the ANTIC chip on the Atari 800 from 1979.)
- RTX / Ray tracing tech. It's only finally getting steam, and RT has been something "just around the corner" for decades (see the Ray Traced Juggler demo for the Commodore Amiga from the 1980s).
- Geforce 8000 series; Nvidia's first time going from the very low end to the very high end, with strong price/performance cards that put AMD/ATi on the backfoot.

Dishonorable mentions:

- ~ 2003 - Nvidia FX series GPUs; the top end FX5800 model was known as "The Dust Buster" because it sounded as loud as a very powerful vacuum available at the time under load. The power consumption was higher than expected and the cooling systems were unable to keep up. FX 5200 was so stripped down it was no faster than any Geforce from years prior.

- Geforce GTX 970 lawsuit; the card was advertised as 4GB, but the design meant 0.5GB of that 4GB was very slow and Nvidia paid every owner of the card $30 because of this

- Geforce RTX 4080 12GB unlaunch; Nvidia "unlaunched" a card because of poor naming and pushback from consumers
